subject: Chemistry
title: Why Rubber Bounces
description: Learn Why Rubber Bounces in one minute.

hook.text: Rubber bounces because its tangled polymer chains stretch and snap back like molecular springs.

buildup.text: Rubber is made of long, coiled polyisoprene chains. At rest, they're tangled in random coils.

discovery.text: When compressed, the chains straighten. They store elastic energy and spring back to their coiled state.

twist.text: Natural rubber gets sticky when hot and brittle when cold. Vulcanization with sulfur fixes both problems.

climax.text: Super balls contain polybutadiene, which returns 92% of impact energy. Almost a perfect bounce.

punchline.text: Tangled chains compress and spring back. Elasticity is molecular.

quiz.question: Why does rubber bounce?
options: Tangled polymer chains store elastic energy when compressed and spring back
Air trapped inside rubber cushions the impact

details.summary: Rubber bounces because it is an elastomer with long, tangled polymer chains that can stretch and return to their original shape. When a rubber ball hits a surface, kinetic energy is stored as potential energy in the deformed polymer chains, which then snap back and launch the ball upward.
details.whyItMatters: Rubber elasticity is a key concept in polymer science. Understanding how molecular structure creates macroscopic properties like bounce explains the behavior of everything from tires to medical devices.
takeaways: Rubber polymers store kinetic energy as elastic potential energy on impact
Cross-links between chains allow deformation and recovery without breaking
Vulcanization adds sulfur cross-links that improve bounce and durability

faq.question: Why does a rubber ball lose height with each bounce?
faq.answer: Not all kinetic energy converts back to motion. Some energy dissipates as heat due to internal friction between polymer chains during deformation. This energy loss is called hysteresis. A perfectly elastic material would bounce forever, but real rubber always converts some energy to heat.

faq.question: How did vulcanization change the usefulness of rubber?
faq.answer: Natural rubber is sticky when warm and brittle when cold. Charles Goodyear discovered that heating rubber with sulfur creates cross-links between polymer chains. These cross-links maintain elasticity across temperatures, making rubber durable and practical for tires, seals, and hundreds of products.
